title: Flavor--Kinetic Entanglement Production from Decay and Scattering at Finite Density
authors: Zekun Li, Jia Liu, Xiao-Ping Wang, Jing-Jun Zhang
abstract: We extend the scattering-entanglement dictionary to finite-density environments by investigating the flavor--kinetic bipartition of the Hilbert space. We show that tracing over kinematic degrees of freedom maps the total branch-changing transition probability directly onto the leading flavor--kinetic linear entanglement entropy. At finite density, the vacuum branch-changing probability is replaced by an occupation-weighted collision probability, built from the same directed reaction-density kernel that enters the integrated Boltzmann equation. The resulting observable is the bath-averaged flavor--kinetic entanglement entropy of a pair sampled from the medium. As a proof of principle, this framework is applied to an $O(N)$ singlet-scalar extended model to probe thermal phase transitions. In the examples studied, the resulting entanglement entropy serves as a collision-based phase-transition-type diagnostic, exhibiting a finite discontinuity across a first-order phase transition and a nonanalytic temperature derivative for continuous transitions. These examples suggest a novel way to characterize thermal phase structures, distinct from traditional thermodynamic order parameters.
summary: This work develops a method to calculate flavor–kinetic entanglement entropy in dense, thermal media by adapting tools from scattering theory. This entanglement measure is shown to be directly proportional to collision rates derived from kinetic equations. Crucially, this diagnostic tool can characterize phase transitions—both first-order and continuous—in a manner distinct from traditional thermodynamic order parameters.
main_problem: The research aims to extend quantum information tools, specifically entanglement entropy, from vacuum processes to finite-density, non-equilibrium environments like the early universe.
main_result: The flavor–kinetic entanglement entropy serves as a novel collision-based diagnostic tool capable of detecting phase transitions by exhibiting distinct discontinuities or nonanalytic temperature derivatives.
method: The authors relate the entanglement entropy to an occupation-weighted collision probability derived from the directed reaction-density kernel used in kinetic theory (Boltzmann equation).
model_or_system: The framework is applied to general particle decay and scattering processes, using a specific flavor–kinetic bipartition of the Hilbert space. A proof-of-principle application uses an O(N) singlet-scalar extended model.
key_observables: Flavor–Kinetic Entanglement Entropy ($E_{fk}$), collision probabilities, and reaction density kernels ($\Gamma$).
important_parameters: Finite particle density, temperature (T), coupling constants, and the characteristic time scales of scattering/decay processes.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on tracing over kinematic degrees of freedom to obtain the leading entanglement entropy, and it assumes an incoherent kinetic ensemble for the background state.
paper_structure: The paper builds from extending the scattering-entanglement dictionary to finite density by defining the flavor–kinetic bipartition. It derives $E_{fk}$ in terms of collision probabilities, applies this diagnostic tool to an O(N) model, and analyzes how the resulting entropy signals phase transitions.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete link between quantum information measures (entanglement) and macroscopic thermodynamic/kinetic properties (phase transitions), offering a new type of order parameter for non-equilibrium systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Benchmark finite-density flavor–kinetic entanglement entropy. Panel (a) shows the first-order benchmark, where bEfk(T) jumps across Tc. Panel (b) shows the continuous benchmark, where bEfk(T) itself remains continuous. Panel (c) shows the corresponding nonanalytic behavior in the first temperature derivative. Dashed and dotted curves are channel-family components of the same entanglement-entropy sum, not independent entropy definitions.

FIG. 2. Parameter scans of the signed dimensionless jump Jfk. Panels (a) and (b) show light-singlet scans for µS = 50 GeV and 100 GeV. The color maps show Jfk = bEfk(Tbro) −1, and green dashed contours mark |Jfk| = 0.02 when that level lies in the plotted range. Black markers denote the independently computed boundary between first-order and continuous transitions from the finite-temperature effective potential. Panel (c) shows the heavy-singlet slice for µS = 400 GeV. There the potential scan finds no FOPT region in the plotted domain, and the signed jump Jfk remains close to zero throughout.
